chunks: Interfacing with SPI slaves. The question: How to interface with slaves?
Talking to an SPI slave means following a short routine that the chip's datasheet describes. SPI itself only moves bits, so each chip defines its own commands.
You set up the master to match the chip's clock mode and speed. Then you pick the chip, send a command, send or collect the data, and let go of the chip.
Picture asking a librarian for a book. You walk up (chip select goes low). You say the shelf code (the command).
Then you hold out your hands (dummy bytes), and the librarian places the book in them (the reply). You walk away (chip select goes high).
The key detail is that the librarian can only answer after hearing the code. So whatever came back while you were still speaking is meaningless. The real answer arrives afterward.
First byte on MOSI is 0x8 farads (read, address 0x0 farads); MISO is don't-care during this byte. The slave drives MISO only during the second byte, here 0x33.
CS stays low for both bytes; the master sends dummy data (don't-care) on MOSI in the second byte.
Datasheet: the chip maker's document that lists the mode, maximum speed and commands. SPI mode: which clock edge samples each bit. The master must match the chip.
Register: a numbered storage cell inside the chip that holds a setting or a reading.
Dummy byte: throwaway data the master sends just to generate clock ticks, so the slave's reply can shift back.
Chip select (CS): the wire that picks the slave and keeps the transfer together.
Say you want to read a chip's ID register at address 0x0 farads. (Numbers starting with "0x" are hexadecimal, a short way to write a byte.)
The datasheet says to set the top bit of the address to mean "read", so the command byte is 0x8 farads. Pull CS low. Send 0x8 farads.
The byte that comes back during this step means nothing. Next, send one dummy byte, 0x00. The byte that comes back now is the register's value, say 0x33. Raise CS.
That is the whole idea.
"I read the datasheet for mode, max clock, bit order and word size, and configure the master.
A transaction is: pull CS low, clock out a command, then for a write clock out data, and for a read clock out dummy bytes while capturing the reply on MISO, then raise CS.
I watch the mode matching, that the reply usually arrives a byte after the command, and that CS stays low for the whole transaction with proper timing.
With several slaves only one CS is low at a time."
Quick check. In an SPI register read, what does the master clock out during the second byte?
